source.title_on_document: The Impact of AI-Generated Text on the Internet

paper_design_summary: The authors draw monthly samples of newly archived English-language websites from the Internet Archive (August 2022 to May 2025), classify each page's text with the Pangram v3 AI-text detector, and correlate a monthly aggregate AI-likelihood score with monthly signals, including average pairwise semantic-embedding similarity and character 3-gram stylistic similarity. A separate Prolific survey of US adults records agreement with six hypotheses about AI text on the internet; no person receives AI assistance and no creative task is assigned.

studies.label: Web-scale corpus analysis of Internet Archive websites (RQ2, RQ3)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. Websites were sampled from the Wayback Machine and classified by an AI-text detector; monthly signals are correlated with the monthly aggregate AI-likelihood score.
assignment.quote: For each hypothesis, we define a measurable signal, compute it for each monthly sample of websites, and test whether it correlates with the aggregate AI likelihood score across months.

participants.exclusions: Pages whose longest paragraph has fewer than 100 words are excluded; only English text is retained (p. 7-8, Section 3.1). Appendix D: one URL per host, target of 10,000 URLs per month, first capture must return HTTP 200 text/html (p. 33). The number of websites analyzed per month or in total is not stated.
participants.who: No participants. The units are websites (archived web pages) first archived from 2022 onward, sampled in 33 monthly intervals from August 2022 to May 2025.
participants.country: Not restricted by country; English-language web pages
participants.quote: We sample websites from the Internet Archive spanning 33 monthly intervals from August 2022 to May 2025.

ai_tool.name_model: Not a treatment. AI use is detected after the fact with the Pangram v3 API (fully AI-generated, AI-assisted, human-written fractions).
ai_tool.how_used: Website authors may or may not have used generative AI; the paper infers AI involvement from the Pangram v3 detector. The aggregate AI likelihood score combines the fully AI-generated and AI-assisted fractions (p. 9, Section 3.3).

task.description: Real web text (visible text of archived websites; the longest paragraph of each page is used as the text sample). No task was assigned.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity (Hypothesis 1, Semantic Contraction): average pairwise cosine similarity of document embeddings within a monthly sample
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings (384 dimensions), L2-normalized; all pairwise cosine similarities for monthly samples with n <= 500 documents, otherwise up to 10,000 randomly sampled pairs (p. 9). Monthly signal correlated with the monthly aggregate AI likelihood score by Pearson correlation (p. 10-11).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Months with higher aggregate AI likelihood score
contrasts.control_arm: Months with lower aggregate AI likelihood score
contrasts.reported: Pearson correlation between monthly average semantic similarity and aggregate AI likelihood: rho = 0.47, p = 0.004 (higher similarity = lower diversity; sign reversed relative to diversity).
contrasts.locator: p. 2, Section 1 (Semantic Contraction Hypothesis); p. 4, Figure 2(a)

contrasts.treatment_arm: Websites predicted to be AI-generated or AI-assisted
contrasts.reported: Across all evaluated months, average semantic similarity between websites predicted to be AI-generated or AI-assisted was 33% higher than that of non-AI websites (semantic similarity scores of 0.0701 vs. 0.0526). No standard error or test reported.

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of document-level semantic embeddings within each monthly sample
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of documents within a monthly sample (n <= 500), or up to 10,000 randomly sampled pairs for larger samples
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Pearson correlation across monthly samples with its p-value; no uncertainty reported for the AI vs non-AI similarity comparison
diversity_detail.notes: Figure 2(a) x-axis starts at 2022-06 although Section 3.1 says sampling runs from August 2022. The number of documents per monthly sample is not stated.

outcomes.name: Stylistic similarity (Hypothesis 6, Stylistic Monoculture): average pairwise character 3-gram Jaccard similarity within a monthly sample
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Set of unique character 3-grams from the first 2,000 lowercased characters of each document; pairwise Jaccard similarity; all pairs for samples with n <= 100, otherwise up to 10,000 random pairs (p. 10). Section 1 (p. 4) instead describes the signal as 'the average pairwise cosine similarity of document writing style embeddings'.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Months with higher aggregate AI likelihood score
contrasts.control_arm: Months with lower aggregate AI likelihood score
contrasts.reported: Pearson correlation: rho = 0.24, p = 0.17 (null not rejected). The panel title inside Figure 16(a) prints rho=0.106, p=0.5368, which differs from the text and caption.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 1 (Stylistic Monoculture Hypothesis); p. 32, Appendix C, Figure 16(a)

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise Jaccard similarity of character 3-gram sets within each monthly sample
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of documents within a monthly sample (n <= 100), or up to 10,000 randomly drawn pairs for larger samples
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Pearson correlation across monthly samples with its p-value
diversity_detail.notes: Internal inconsistency in how the measure is described (style embeddings on p. 4 vs character 3-gram Jaccard on p. 10 and p. 32) and in the reported correlation (rho = 0.24, p = 0.17 in text and caption vs rho = 0.106, p = 0.5368 in the Figure 16(a) panel title).

studies.label: Participant survey of US adults on beliefs about AI text on the internet (RQ1)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants completed one of three survey parts, each covering a subset of the six hypotheses; the paper does not say how participants were allocated to parts. No AI assistance was given.
assignment.quote: The study was administered as an online form in three parts, each corresponding to a subset of the six hypotheses.

participants.exclusions: Not stated. Part 1 (Hypotheses 1-3) n = 303, Part 2 (Hypotheses 4 and 6) n = 301, Part 3 (Hypothesis 5) n = 299; N = 903 responses from 853 unique participants. The 853 is the count of people whose responses were collected; the paper does not state a separate analyzed count.
participants.who: US adults recruited through Prolific, stratified to be representative by age, sex, and ethnicity; mean age 45.4 (SD = 15.73).
participants.quote: In total, N = 903 responses were collected from 853 unique participants.

ai_tool.how_used: None. Participants rated agreement with hypothesis statements on a 7-point Likert scale and reported AI-use frequency and views of AI.

task.description: Survey of beliefs (7-point agreement with statements about AI text on the internet). No creative output is produced or scored.

company_involvement.description: Two authors (Sawood Alam, Mark Graham) are affiliated with the Internet Archive, which supplied the data. Pangram provided a research grant supporting use of its API; the authors state Pangram had no role in design, analysis, or the decision to publish and that they applied for the grant after choosing the detector.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations; p. 11, Acknowledgements and Competing Interests

eligibility.reason: No person is assigned to AI assistance. S1 is an observational corpus study of real websites that correlates the monthly detected share of AI-generated or AI-assisted text with across-document semantic and stylistic similarity, which fits the observational context class (real output compared across time with a similarity outcome). Criterion 2 is not met for S1 because its units are websites and monthly samples, not people; the S2 survey has 853 people but measures beliefs only, with no AI assistance and no scored output. Criterion 3 is met only in the sense that S1's similarity measures are computed on real text.

one_line_finding: Across monthly Internet Archive samples (August 2022 to May 2025), the detected AI-likelihood score correlates positively with average pairwise semantic-embedding similarity (rho = 0.47, p = 0.004; AI vs non-AI websites 0.0701 vs 0.0526) but not significantly with character 3-gram stylistic similarity (rho = 0.24, p = 0.17), pp. 2 and 4.
open_questions: Is the AI-classified vs non-AI website similarity comparison (0.0701 vs 0.0526, p. 2) better coded as ai_vs_human context? The AI group includes AI-assisted (human-written with AI involvement) pages, so I coded it as an observational adopter vs non-adopter comparison.
Figure 16(a) panel title prints rho=0.106, p=0.5368 while the text and caption give rho = 0.24, p = 0.17 (p. 4, p. 32). Which is correct?
The Hypothesis 6 measure is described as writing style embeddings on p. 4 but as character 3-gram Jaccard similarity in Methods (p. 10) and Figure 16 (p. 32).

Sampling window: Methods say 33 monthly intervals from August 2022 to May 2025 (p. 7), while the x-axes of Figures 2(a), 3(a), and 16(a) start at 2022-06. The number of documents per monthly sample is not stated.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they do not bear on creativity or diversity: factual error rate (Hyp. 2, with 50 Prolific fact-checking annotators, p. 10), positive-sentiment rate (Hyp. 3, rho = 0.56, p = 0.0003), outbound link density (Hyp. 4, rho = -0.12, p = 0.48), and Gzip compression ratio (Hyp. 5, rho = -0.02, p = 0.89). The fact-checking annotators (N = 50 after excluding 11 timed-out submissions) are raters within S1, not a separate study. Appendix A is a detector robustness evaluation with AI-generated and human-written text samples, not people. The headline prevalence figure is 'roughly 35%' of new websites AI-generated or AI-assisted by mid-2025 (abstract, p. 1).
